opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few, and the interesting thing is that the technical modeling problem is often not the hardest one.

The first is choosing the right problem. A lot of the impact we've seen, whether it's protein structure prediction or materials discovery, came from picking problems where there was a clear, well-defined objective, a way to measure progress, and a real community that cared about the answer. If you pick a problem where you can't tell whether you've succeeded, it's very hard for AI to make a difference, because you can't train against it or validate it.

The second is data. People say "data is the bottleneck" so often it sounds like a cliché, but it's true in a specific way. It's not just quantity, it's quality, consistency, and coverage. Protein structure worked partly because decades of experimental work had gone into the Protein Data Bank, carefully curated. Many scientific fields don't have that. The data is scattered across labs, in different formats, often with negative results never recorded. So a big part of the job is building the datasets, or finding clever ways to generate them, through simulation, self-distillation, or closing the loop with experiments.

The third, and maybe the most underappreciated, is the last mile: getting from a model's prediction to something scientists actually trust and use. A prediction is only valuable if someone acts on it. That means the model has to tell you how confident it is, so you know when to believe it. It has to be accessible, which is why releasing tools and databases openly has mattered so much. And it has to fit into how scientists actually work. Often you need experimental validation, and the wet lab moves much slower than the model. That mismatch between how fast we can generate hypotheses and how fast we can test them is becoming a real constraint.

Finally, there's people and culture. The best results come from teams where machine learning researchers and domain scientists work side by side and each understands enough of the other's world to ask the right questions. That kind of collaboration is still rarer than it should be, and building it is as important as building the next model.

r001.rationale: It says predictions often need experimental validation and that the slower pace of wet-lab testing constrains impact.

r002.rationale: It identifies accessibility and fit with scientists’ workflows as necessary for people to trust and use model predictions.

r003.rationale: It discusses confidence and validation, but does not say that pursuing an incorrect prediction can waste substantial researcher effort.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute AlphaFold’s widespread adoption to communicating prediction reliability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that the bottleneck has shifted. For a long time the question was whether these models could do anything useful for science at all. With AlphaFold, with the work in materials and weather and mathematics, I think that question is largely settled. So the hard problems now are less about raw capability and more about everything that surrounds it.

The first big one is data. People sometimes assume that because the internet is enormous, science must be swimming in data too. It isn't, not in the form that matters. Protein structures worked because decades of crystallographers deposited their results in the Protein Data Bank in a standardized, open way. Most fields don't have that. Experimental results sit in lab notebooks, negative results never get published, and the data that does exist is noisy and inconsistently labeled. So in many domains the limiting factor is not the model, it's whether anyone has built the equivalent of the PDB.

The second is the gap between prediction and verification. A model can propose a million candidate molecules or materials overnight, but you can't synthesize and test a million things overnight. Experiments are slow, expensive, and often bespoke. So unless we close that loop, with automated labs, better simulators, or much smarter ways of choosing which experiments to run, the AI side will simply outrun the physical side and most of its output will sit unverified. I actually think this is where some of the most important work over the next few years will happen.

The third is that scientific progress is a human and institutional process, not just a technical one. For a prediction to become a drug or a new material, it has to be trusted by domain experts, pass through regulatory systems, and be adopted by people with their own incentives and workflows. Models that are right but opaque struggle here. So interpretability, calibrated uncertainty, and genuinely working alongside scientists rather than handing them a black box all matter enormously.

And then finally there is the question of what counts as a discovery. A lot of today's systems are very good at interpolating within the space of what we already know. The really transformative stuff, the new hypotheses, the conceptual leaps, that is still much harder, and I would be cautious about anyone who claims we've solved it. So the honest answer is that the bottlenecks are data, the experimental loop, trust and integration, and the frontier of genuine novelty. The exciting part is that each of those is tractable, and they are the right problems to be stuck on.

r001.rationale: The response says AI-generated candidates must be synthesized and tested, and calls the gap between prediction and verification a major bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It identifies adoption by scientists, trust, and fit with their workflows as factors that limit AI’s impact.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that an inaccurate prediction could cause an individual researcher to waste substantial effort pursuing it.

r004.rationale: It mentions AlphaFold’s success and the Protein Data Bank, but does not attribute its adoption to indicating prediction reliability.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is the gap between making a prediction and demonstrating that it actually leads to something useful. You can have a model that proposes a promising molecule or a new material, but somebody still has to make it, test it, and establish whether it works under real-world conditions.

So we need to think about the whole discovery process. Where does the data come from? How reliable is it? Can we run the experiments that would tell us whether the model is right? And can those experimental results feed back into the model? In many areas, that loop is still quite slow.

There’s also a question of choosing the right problems. A technically impressive result doesn’t necessarily remove the bottleneck that scientists actually face. That requires very close collaboration with people who understand the science and the practical constraints.

For me, the opportunity is to bring those pieces together: models, experiments, and domain expertise. The measure of success has to be whether we’ve enabled a discovery or an application that matters, rather than simply improved performance on a benchmark.

r001.rationale: It says proposed molecules or materials still need to be made and tested under real-world conditions to establish whether they work.

r002.rationale: It mentions collaboration with domain experts and practical constraints, but does not identify users’ ability to use the technology as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that an accurate system could still cause a researcher to spend substantial effort pursuing an incorrect prediction.

r004.rationale: It does not mention AlphaFold or prediction reliability as a reason for its widespread adoption.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest bottlenecks is closing the loop between a prediction and a real scientific advance. An AI system might suggest a promising molecule or material, but you still need to make it, measure its properties, and establish whether it actually solves the problem you care about. Accelerating one step doesn’t necessarily accelerate that whole process.

A second challenge is knowing what to ask the system to optimize. The properties we can easily measure aren’t always the properties that matter in practice. You need scientists working closely with the people developing the models to define the right questions and the right tests.

And then there’s validation. Where does the model work reliably, and where should you be skeptical? Making these tools impactful requires experimental feedback, clear evidence of their limitations, and tools that scientists can actually use in their everyday work.

r001.rationale: The response says predictions must be made and measured experimentally to determine whether they solve the scientific problem.

r002.rationale: It identifies tools scientists can use in everyday work as necessary for impact.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that a researcher could waste substantial effort pursuing an incorrect prediction.

r004.rationale: It discusses assessing model reliability generally, but does not mention AlphaFold or explain its adoption.
